body: Every way of travelling has built a place for its pause. The caravanserai gave a day’s march its courtyard, the coaching inn gave the stagecoach its supper and its bed, and the railway gave the city its station. The airport made waiting into a building type of its own, and the highway gave the car its service area. Each was sized to the time its pause allowed, and the longer the pause, the more public the building became.

Road transport is now changing faster than at any time since the car replaced the horse. Vehicles are going electric, and in a few cities they have begun to drive themselves. Together these shifts are building a new road transport system, and its pause is changing with it. A car that once stopped for five minutes to fill its tank now stops for twenty minutes to an hour to charge, and a truck or a bus can stop for a whole night. Yet the places built for charging have hardly moved on from the forecourts they replaced: a row of posts at the edge of the tarmac, and a driver waiting in the car.

This thesis proposes the Powerhouse, an architecture for that pause. At its centre is the charger. Around it is a network of programmes chosen for the neighbourhood, and around that, public space open to everyone. The programme brings people in; the charge lets them stay. It is built for everyone who drives, and for anyone who reaches it on foot, by bus or by bicycle.

Thousands of charging sites will be built over the coming decades, and most are being planned as infrastructure and nothing more. This chapter asks what they could become if they were designed for the people who stop there rather than only for their vehicles. It starts from a simple belief: that the energy transition is a chance to leave behind a better and greener landscape than the one we have now.

Transport uses a great deal of energy, and wastes most of it. Of every hundred tonnes of greenhouse gas the United States emits, twenty-eight come from moving people and goods, more than from any other sector.<sup>1</sup> Much of the problem is the engine. Fill a petrol car and roughly seven-tenths of that energy leaves through the exhaust and the radiator as heat; only about three-tenths moves the car. An electric car turns the ratio around, putting close to nine-tenths of what is in its battery to work.<sup>2</sup> It makes the same journey on about a third of the energy. It is only as clean as the grid behind it, though. A decade ago, economists who priced the damage from driving electric across the United States found a clear benefit in California and a net harm in coal-heavy states.<sup>3</sup> This is one reason the Powerhouse makes and stores its own energy.

The shift is happening quickly. In 2020 the world bought around three million electric cars; in 2025 it bought more than twenty million.<sup>4</sup> In the United States there were about seven million electric cars and light trucks on the road in 2025, under three in every hundred. The Energy Information Administration expects about 120 million by 2040, close to four in ten.<sup>5</sup> Speed is not the same as certainty. A review of ninety-four studies on electric-car adoption found that what actually persuades people to switch, public charging included, is far less settled than is usually assumed.<sup>6</sup> Behind electrification, automation is arriving too, as driverless taxis carry paying passengers in American cities and freight follows. This thesis treats it as background: with a driver or without one, every electric vehicle has to stop to charge.

For now, most of that charging happens at home. By the Department of Energy’s estimate, four of every five charges happen in a driveway or a garage.<sup>7</sup> The convenience has a cost. An electric car driven a typical American distance uses three to four thousand kilowatt-hours of electricity a year, about a third of what an average home already uses.<sup>8</sup> Home charging moves the cost of the transition onto household bills, and it is no option at all for people who live in apartments or keep their car on the street. As the fleet grows, public charging will have to carry more of the load, and the places built for it will shape how millions of people spend part of their week.

body: The railway understood the pause. The great stations of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries were among the grandest civic buildings in their cities: passengers arrived early and waited in halls, concourses and plazas lined with restaurants, shops and newsstands. In New York, McKim, Mead and White borrowed the vaults of a Roman bath for the waiting room of Pennsylvania Station in 1910, and when the station was demolished in 1963 the city lost its great civic room and its preservation movement began.<sup>9</sup> The airport went further and made the terminal a city of waiting.

The road went the other way. For most of the twentieth century its pause was the gas station, which settled early into a formula that hardly changed afterwards: a canopy over the pumps, islands to pull up beside, and a booth to pay at on the way out.<sup>10</sup> It was built for five minutes, and it did that well. Five minutes is long enough to pay and too short for a civic form.

Charging has inherited this form without its reason. The usual response is a few chargers added to the edge of an existing forecourt or car park. The federal standards behind the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure programme set out power, connectors and uptime, and say nothing about the place around the charger.<sup>11</sup> So drivers sit in their cars beside a row of posts for half an hour. Freight is worse off. Truck parking already ranks as the American trucking industry’s second most pressing problem, after the economy, and drivers near the end of their legal hours often keep driving in search of a space.<sup>12</sup> Charging for heavy vehicles is scarcer still, and a recent review of the American market names it, with range and upfront cost, as one of the main obstacles to electric freight.<sup>13</sup> Marc Augé’s word for such places fits them well: non-places, used all the time and belonging to no one.<sup>14</sup> The geographer Peter Merriman has argued that the label is too quick. Writing on England’s first motorway and its service areas, he shows that such sites are made into places by the people, vehicles and practices that pass through them.<sup>15</sup> The charging stop is not condemned to be a non-place; it has simply never been designed as anything else.

A few places show that the pause can hold more. In England, Gridserve’s electric forecourt at Braintree opened in 2020 with a café, a shop and a lounge beside its chargers, a first sign of what a longer stop can support.16 In Los Angeles, Tesla has built a diner beside a Supercharger. Can Aktuna’s study of it describes how such sites borrow from hospitality, leisure and spectacle to make “compulsory waiting” more inhabitable, and finds that drivers respond to the branded spectacle with ambivalence and that experiences like it are unevenly spread.17 These are commercial answers. The demand they reveal is public. Japan has done it at national scale. Since 1993 its Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism has designated more than 1,200 michi-no-eki, “road stations”, each pairing round-the-clock rest and toilets for travellers with a market for local produce, restaurants, crafts, events and disaster relief, run with the town and its residents.18 The road station is the closest thing the road has to the railway station’s civic room. The Powerhouse asks what that room becomes when the pause is a charge.

body: A charge stop lasts as long as the battery takes to fill, which depends on the size of the battery and the power of the charger. A fast charger can take a car from low to most of the way full in twenty minutes to an hour. A slower charger of the kind found at homes, workplaces and bus depots takes several hours, and usually runs overnight.<sup>19</sup> Larger vehicles carry larger batteries and stop for longer, so the same pause stretches from a coffee for a car to a night’s sleep for a bus.

For freight, the stop is set by law as well as by technology. American rules require a truck driver to take thirty minutes off after eight hours at the wheel, and ten hours off duty at the end of a working day.<sup>20</sup> An electric truck can charge during a break its driver already has to take, which turns a regulation into a reason to build.

The charge stop is therefore not one stop but many. Cars, trucks, buses, motorcycles, bicycles and e-bikes all need somewhere to charge, and each brings a different person to the site for a different length of time: twenty minutes, an hour or two, a whole night. A gas station could treat every visitor the same, because everyone left within five minutes. A charge stop cannot. Its length is what makes it worth designing, and its range, from twenty minutes to overnight, is what the Powerhouse plans for.

body: A long pause gives a site time, but not a reason to be there. The Powerhouse takes its ground from parking, the space every vehicle already claims wherever it stops; a typical car stands still for about ninety-five per cent of its life.<sup>21</sup> But a charger set on that ground does not make a place, any more than a bench makes a park. What the ground needs is something to do.

Space alone has been tried. For more than sixty years New York has let developers build taller in return for a plaza or an arcade at street level. When Jerold Kayden’s team surveyed 503 of these spaces, they rated about two in every five as marginal: open, public, and empty.<sup>22</sup> William Whyte spent years filming people in plazas like these. They stayed where there was something to do and somewhere to sit, and walked past everywhere else.<sup>23</sup> Ray Oldenburg called the places that hold people between home and work “third places”: the café, the barbershop, the corner bar.<sup>24</sup> A 2025 study that monitored young adults’ brain activity and stress found that such places restore people about as well as green space does, mainly through the contact they allow with others.<sup>25</sup> Eric Klinenberg’s term for the libraries, parks and community rooms that make this contact possible is social infrastructure.<sup>26</sup>

That is the role of the programme at the Powerhouse. It is chosen for each site, from what the people who live, work and travel nearby lack: a gym, a clinic, a library, a market, rooms for drivers. It is what brings people in, whether they arrive with a vehicle to charge or on foot from the street. The charge is what lets them stay. Part of every site is open to anyone, with nothing to buy, so that the Powerhouse reads first as a public building and only second as a place to charge.
notes: Donald Shoup, The High Cost of Free Parking (Chicago: Planners Press, 2005).

William H. Whyte, The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces (Washington, DC: Conservation Foundation, 1980).

body: If the programme brings people in, the charger is what holds the network of programmes together. It sits at the centre, and everything around it is arranged by how long people stay. Closest to it is what fits twenty minutes: somewhere to sit, eat, wash and let children play. Further out is what fits an hour or two: a gym, a clinic, a reading room, a place to work. Furthest out, on corridors and at depots, is what fits a night: rooms, showers and a kitchen for drivers. Each ring serves the people charging, and each is open to people who are not.

Stan Allen argued that infrastructure works best as a field: it fixes the services and leaves the uses free to change.27 The charger works the same way. It brings vehicles to the same place every day, it fixes the time they stay, and it brings energy, made and stored on site, to everything around it. The programmes can change with the neighbourhood while the charger at the centre stays put. On a freight corridor the network might be rooms and showers; in a city, a gym and a workspace; in a town, a clinic and a market. The michi-no-eki show the same pattern at a national scale: one standard core of rest and toilets, and around it whatever each town chooses to add.18

The network also works between sites. No two Powerhouses carry the same programme, because no two neighbourhoods lack the same things, but every one has a charger at its centre and public space at its edge. Together they make a network across the road system as well as within each site.
notes: Stan Allen, “Infrastructural Urbanism,” in Points + Lines: Diagrams and Projects for the City (New York: Princeton Architectural Press, 1999), 46–57.

body: The proposition comes out of the sections above. Electric road transport is growing quickly, and its pause is longer than the one the road was built for. Today that pause is spent in non-places. Programme, not space, is what holds people, and a charger can sit at the centre of a network of programmes chosen for each neighbourhood. Put together, this is the hypothesis: an Electric Vehicle Powerhouse complex will turn charging activities into an opportunity for enhanced civic and community engagement. If the extra time leads only to more retail, the hypothesis fails.

Three questions test it, and each becomes a chapter. Chapter 2, The Conditions of the Pause, asks how long each kind of vehicle stays, from a quick charge to an overnight rest, and what that time allows. Chapter 3, The Place, asks what makes people stay and what each neighbourhood lacks. Chapter 4, The Framework, asks how programme, public space and charging fit together on one site, measured as minutes on site, the share of the site open to all, and the programme it holds. The method is comparative: existing gas stations, service areas, truck stops and charging hubs are read on these three measures, in corridor, city and town settings.

The research starts in New York and widens to the rest of the United States, with precedents from the United Kingdom, Europe and Japan. It covers every road vehicle and the people nearby who do not charge at all, and every stay from a twenty-minute charge to a driver’s overnight rest. Chargers at malls and supermarkets are set aside, because there the shopping draws the charger rather than the other way round. Faster charging does not undo the argument. In 2025 BYD announced a charging system that adds about 400 kilometres of range in five minutes,<sup>28</sup> but the Powerhouse does not depend on a slow charge. It depends on a programme worth staying for.
notes: Reuters, “BYD Unveils New Super-Charging EV Tech, to Build Charging Network in China,” March 17, 2025, https://www.reuters.com/business/autos-transportation/chinas-byd-unveils-faster-charging-ev-platform-aims-build-over-4000-charging-2025-03-17/.

body: Three ways of reading run through the chapters that follow. Each is suited to one part of the Powerhouse: sustainability to its ground and energy, phenomenology to the pause itself, and social theory to who the place is for.

Sustainable development is usually defined as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own.<sup>29</sup> At the Powerhouse it has three parts. Environmentally, it builds on ground vehicles already claim, and makes and stores its own energy. Socially, it serves people who cannot charge at home and stays open to those who do not charge at all. Architecturally, it lets the energy be seen. Ian McHarg’s method of reading a site in layers, and Sim Van der Ryn and Stuart Cowan’s principle that design should grow from its place and make natural systems visible, guide where a Powerhouse goes and how it shows its power.<sup>30</sup> This lens leads Chapter 2.

Phenomenology asks what it is like to spend the pause on site. Martin Heidegger argued that to build is to make dwelling possible, and that a built thing, like a bridge, gathers a place around it.<sup>31</sup> A charger can gather in the same way. Christian Norberg-Schulz added that people need to know where they are and to feel that they belong,<sup>32</sup> which today’s identical charging sites rarely allow. Read this way, the Powerhouse turns a pause in a journey into a place, and this lens leads Chapter 3.

Social theory asks who the place is for. Henri Lefebvre showed that space is produced: planned by those who design it and lived by those who use it.<sup>33</sup> Charging sites today are almost entirely planned, by standards and operators, and for the vehicle. Lefebvre’s right to the city, the claim that everyone may use and shape urban space,<sup>34</sup> underlies the Powerhouse’s promise of public space open to all. Michel Foucault’s account of surveillance names the opposite risk, a place that watches people and moves on anyone who lingers.<sup>35</sup> Jane Jacobs offers the answer the Powerhouse takes: safety that comes from people being present, not from being watched.<sup>36</sup> This lens leads Chapter 4.

body: Chapter 1 set out the proposition: the programme brings people in; the charge lets them stay. This chapter reads the conditions of that stay: the ground it happens on, how people charge, the buildings that have held a pause before, the vehicles, the rules and the future. It starts with the network as it stands.

A charging network joins electricity supply, charging equipment and vehicles. A station is a location; a port serves one vehicle at a time. Several connectors on one post do not mean several vehicles can charge at once. “Public” describes who may use a charger, not who owns the land under it: a privately run station can be open to any driver, while a depot or workplace can restrict entry.<sup>1</sup> <sup>2</sup> These distinctions matter as soon as a national count is turned into the size of a building.

In October 2026 the federal Alternative Fuels Data Center listed 290,019 charging ports at 88,068 stations across the United States, public and private; Map 1.1 shows where they are. Of these, 260,991 ports at 82,698 stations are public, a little over three ports per station on average. Most of them are slow. About seven in ten public ports are Level 2, the kind that takes hours; about three in ten, 79,030, are DC fast chargers. Half of those fast ports belong to a single network, Tesla’s. The network is also concentrated: California alone holds about a quarter of all public ports, and California, New York and Florida together hold about two in five.<sup>3</sup>

The network has grown quickly. The same database counted 107,561 ports in 2020 and 184,098 in 2023,<sup>4</sup> so today’s total is about 2.7 times what it was five years ago. Fast charging grew fastest: more than 18,000 new fast ports opened in 2025 alone, about 30 per cent more than the year before.<sup>5</sup> Cars have grown faster still. At the end of 2025 there were 33 electric cars for every public charging point in the United States, up from fewer than 20 in 2020.<sup>6</sup> The network is expanding, but the fleet is outrunning it. Set against the 2030 scenario in section 2.2, today’s public fast ports are a little over two-fifths of the modelled need, and today’s public Level 2 ports about one-sixth.

A count of plugs says nothing about the place around them. On average a public station is just over three ports: three vehicle-sized spaces and a post. Nothing in the count says whether there is room for the person who arrives with them. That is the condition this chapter reads, and the one the Powerhouse is meant to change. A gap on a map is not a site. A Powerhouse belongs where a need for charging meets a connection to the road and the electrical grid, and a neighbourhood with a reason to come.

The sections that follow move from that ground to charging practice, then to architectural types, vehicle demand, regulation and the future. New York appears only as a demanding condition within the wider study: one state with about one in thirteen of the nation’s public ports, in a city where half of all car owners park on the street. It is not a site selection. A corridor, a town and a dense city may all need a Powerhouse, but the pause will work differently in each.

body: Roads are usually described by movement: lanes, junctions, speeds and travel times. Yet every trip ends with a vehicle standing still, and the ground built for standing is larger than the ground built for moving. Taken together, the roofs, roads and paved lots of the lower forty-eight states cover about 112,610 square kilometres, slightly less than the area of Ohio.<sup>7</sup> Nobody knows how much of that is parking. One national estimate places the number of parking spaces in the United States anywhere between 105 million and 2 billion;<sup>8</sup> the width of the range is itself the finding.

Where the ground has been counted, the numbers are large. Los Angeles County held about 18.6 million parking spaces in 2010, covering some 200 square miles, or 14 per cent of its incorporated land.<sup>9</sup> An inventory of five American cities found 1.6 million spaces in Seattle, 5.2 for every household; 2.2 million in Philadelphia, 3.7 per household; and 27.1 per household in Jackson, Wyoming.<sup>10</sup> Seen from above, paved surfaces cover about 28 per cent of Sacramento, more than its roofs.<sup>11</sup>

This ground is sized to the vehicle, not to the person in it. It is laid out for turning circles and clearances, used a few minutes or hours at a time, and empty for much of the day, since a typical car stands still about 95 per cent of its life, as Chapter 1 noted. It is also hard ground. It heats in the sun and sheds rainwater quickly, which is why the EPA’s Green Streets Handbook treats parking surfaces as places to plant, shade and let water soak in.12

The Powerhouse begins on this ground. It is parking in the sense that vehicles already stand there, but the proposal is not a parking lot with a building beside it. The ground is reorganised around a place people can enter. A charger stays reachable by a vehicle; a room, court or garden is reachable without one, and the two routes meet without asking anyone on foot to cross a working charging bay. The US Access Board’s guidance on accessible charging makes the same point at the scale of one person: clear space and an accessible route to the facilities, not only to the plug.<sup>13</sup>

This also suggests where a Powerhouse can stand, without naming a site. The ground already exists wherever vehicles stop: at the curb, in the depot, on the forecourt, at the service area and in the garage. A Powerhouse belongs where that ground meets a need for charging, a connection to the road and the electrical grid, and a neighbourhood with a reason to come. New York shows the opposite extreme to Jackson. It has the least parking per household of the five cities counted,<sup>14</sup> and half of its car owners park on the street.<sup>15</sup> Where ground for standing is this scarce, a shared place to charge matters most.

body: Charging is not one activity. At home it happens while someone is doing something else; at work it can fill the working day; at a destination it goes along with a visit. A fast-charging stop interrupts a journey, and depot charging follows a vehicle’s shift. The architecture depends on which of these sets the timetable, and a long connection does not have to mean a long wait beside the car.

Most charging is private. Worldwide, electric-vehicle owners surveyed by the IEA charge at home or at work almost 75 per cent of the time and use public fast chargers about 10 per cent of the time. Public provision is still growing quickly: there were more than seven million public charging points at the end of 2025, after growth of more than a third that year.<sup>16</sup> These are global figures; Chapter 1 gives the American one, four in five charges at home.

There are three kinds of charger: Level 1, Level 2 and DC fast. The US Department of Transportation’s examples for a passenger car run from about 4–10 hours on Level 2 to between 20 minutes and an hour on a fast charger.<sup>17</sup> The real time depends on the car and the session. A charger’s rating is its maximum, and the temperature, how full the battery already is, the car’s own limits and a supply shared with other chargers can all slow it down.

In 2023 the national laboratory modelled what the United States would need in 2030 for 33 million electric cars and light trucks: 25.7 million ports at single-family homes, 570,000 at apartment buildings, 490,000 at workplaces, about 1.07 million public Level 2 ports and 182,000 public fast ports.<sup>18</sup> It is a planning scenario made in 2023, not a count, and it covers light-duty vehicles only; it does not size a bus or freight network.

For the Powerhouse this narrows the case. Most vehicles should charge where they already spend time. The opportunity is strongest where a visit that has to happen meets a programme worth having: the city driver with nowhere to charge at home, the traveller far from home, the fleet between shifts. The study also has to count the people who arrive without a vehicle, because counting only those who are plugged in would miss the public use the hypothesis is about.

body: Every place of waiting answers the same three questions in plan. How do you enter? Where does the person wait? Where does the vehicle go? The answers have changed with each kind of journey, and reading them side by side shows what the charging stop has inherited and what it has lost.

The oldest answer is the courtyard. A caravanserai was built as a square or rectangular enclosure around an open court, with a single entrance and rooms arranged around the edge.<sup>19</sup> Animals, goods and travellers came through the same gate and shared the same open centre, but the rooms gave each traveller a place out of the way of the traffic. The English coaching inn kept the arrangement and added height. At the George Inn in Southwark, rebuilt in 1677 after a fire, galleries on the upper floors look down onto the yard where coaches once drew in.<sup>20</sup> In both, the vehicle and the person share one ground, and the building wraps around it.

The railway separated them. At Liverpool Road in Manchester, opened in 1830, passengers entered from the street and passed through the station building to reach the trains, so the building became the threshold between the city and the line.<sup>21</sup> By 1913, Grand Central Terminal in New York had turned that threshold into a public room: a concourse between the street and the platforms, open to anyone, where the whole city could cross, meet and wait.<sup>22</sup> The train was out of sight below; the person had the hall.

The road went the other way. In 1913 Pittsburgh got two of the first filling stations built for drivers to pull in to: the Murwin station in June and Gulf’s on Baum Boulevard in December.<sup>23</sup> The type that followed was reduced to its essentials: a canopy over the pumps, an island to stop beside and a small kiosk. The vehicle took the whole site; the person stayed in the car or stood beside it. The Pennsylvania Turnpike, opened in 1940, grouped fuel, food and rest at service plazas along a controlled-access road,<sup>24</sup> which gave the long-distance driver a building again, but one placed beside the road rather than built around the stop.

The airport repeated the railway’s separation at a larger scale. The TWA Flight Center at New York’s Idlewild airport, opened in 1962, made the space between the kerb and the aircraft a single sweeping hall in which waiting was designed as an experience; it is now restored as a hotel, and people still come to sit in it.<sup>25</sup> The most recent case is the electric forecourt. GRIDSERVE’s Braintree site, opened in 2020, puts a building with a café and lounge beside its chargers.<sup>26</sup> It brings back a room for the person, but the plan is still the forecourt’s: bays in front, building to one side.

Read together, the cases show three moves that make a place of waiting work. The first is a protected interior, a court, hall or concourse, that is not the vehicle’s space. The second is a single, legible threshold where arrival becomes a stay. The third is a room sized to the pause. The gas station kept none of the three, and the charging stop has inherited it. The Powerhouse needs all three: a court that people and vehicles share without crossing each other’s paths, a threshold that turns a charging bay into an arrival, and rooms sized to twenty minutes, an hour or two, and a night.

The drawings that follow this section use the same layers for every case: approach, vehicle threshold, pedestrian threshold, waiting space and route back. The dates identify cases; they do not claim that one type grew out of another. The comparison also cannot settle cause and effect on its own: people may stay longer because a place is good, rather than the place being good because people had time. The site study in later chapters tests that with observation.

body: A charge stop has to be read at the scale of the vehicle. A bicycle and a truck may both stay for several hours, but they need very different space, energy and access. Battery size alone does not set the length of the stop: a small battery on a slow charger can take hours, and a large one may take only what the next leg needs.

Table 2.1 compares named vehicles, each under its own charging conditions, so its rows cannot be ranked against one another. Bosch gives about 4.5 hours for its PowerTube 500 e-bike battery on the 4 A Standard Charger.<sup>27</sup> The manual for the 2020 Zero SR/F motorcycle gives under five hours for its ZF14.4 pack in mild conditions; it is an older model, used here as an example.<sup>28</sup> The Department of Transportation’s car examples rest on their own battery and charging assumptions.

The arithmetic is simple once the energy and the average power are stated. Ford’s extended-range E-Transit van has an 89 kWh usable battery.<sup>29</sup> Charging it from 10 to 80 per cent adds 62.3 kWh: about 37 minutes at an average of 100 kW, or about 5.7 hours at 11 kW. These are calculations, not a measured charging curve, but they show why a charge time has to start from the energy added and the average power, rather than the whole battery and the charger’s peak rating.

Larger vehicles follow the same arithmetic. New Flyer gives a full depot charge of 4.9 hours for a 660 kWh bus,<sup>30</sup> and Volvo gives 80 per cent in about 90 minutes for its 565 kWh VNR Electric truck at up to 250 kW.<sup>31</sup> Both are manufacturers’ figures for particular equipment; together they show how widely the stop can vary.

The three stays from Chapter 1 still frame the design: twenty minutes, an hour or two, and a night. They are reference cases, and real sessions will fall between them. For each one the design asks what a person can reach, use and leave comfortably in the time, and keeps the way back to the vehicle short.

Growth changes how many visits a site serves more than how long each one lasts. Section 2.2 gives one scale for cars in 2030. For heavier vehicles, the IEA’s Current Policies Scenario puts electric trucks at about a fifth of global truck sales in 2035 and about a tenth of the trucks on the road.<sup>32</sup> Neither figure says how many chargers one site needs; each Powerhouse will still need its own study of catchment, vehicle schedules and grid connection.

The site study will keep two clocks: how long the vehicle is plugged in, and how long the person stays, from arrival to departure. It will also note whether people leave the site while their vehicle charges. A longer stay counts only if comfort, access and a free programme explain it.

body: Some pauses are set by law, not by the battery. In the United States a truck driver may drive up to eleven hours after ten consecutive hours off duty, and must take a thirty-minute break after eight hours of driving. Time on duty but not driving can count as that break, and there are exceptions and sleeper-berth rules.<sup>33</sup> A charging session is not a required rest in itself, but it can fall within one.

European rules are different. Within their scope, a driver takes a forty-five-minute break after four and a half hours of driving and a regular daily rest of eleven hours, which can be split or shortened in defined ways.<sup>34</sup> These rules set the driver’s working day, not the vehicle’s charging. The design opportunity is to let the two coincide where they can, while keeping a place to rest that does not depend on the plug.

Charging funded under the federal NEVI rules (23 C.F.R. Part 680) has requirements of its own. A corridor fast-charging station must have at least four ports, each able to deliver up to 150 kW at the same time, and must be open to the public around the clock.<sup>35</sup> Each port must also be working more than 97 per cent of the year, by the rule’s own calculation.<sup>36</sup> The rules apply to funded projects within their scope; they do not cover every private charger or promise any particular charging time.

Accessibility is a second layer. The US Access Board’s guidance separates what the law already requires from further design recommendations. An accessible route, usable controls and a clear transfer space have to work together with the route into the building, and no canopy column, cable or vehicle overhang should block that route. The exact requirements depend on the site and are checked once a site is chosen.

Land-use permission is a third. New York City’s City of Yes for Carbon Neutrality amendment, adopted in 2023, changed the zoning rules to make room for energy infrastructure.<sup>37</sup> It does not permit every programme around a charger everywhere. A clinic, a café or overnight rooms may each need their own approvals, occupancy class and fire strategy. The final design has to show permission for the whole building, because no “civic station” category exists yet.

In the comparison, these rules are recorded for each site. If one site gives more ground to the public than another, the reason may be zoning, ownership or access rules rather than the length of the charge. Recording them keeps the study from crediting charging time with an outcome that another rule produced.

body: Charging is getting faster, and it is getting heavier. In March 2025 SAE published J3271, the Megawatt Charging System for trucks and buses, whose connectors can deliver up to 3.75 megawatts.<sup>38</sup> For cars, BYD’s one-megawatt system, mentioned in Chapter 1, adds about 400 kilometres of range in five minutes. A vehicle’s stop will shorten. The power a site must deliver will not. The National Renewable Energy Laboratory expects that charging sites for heavy trucks will need upwards of 20 megawatts.<sup>39</sup> The stop gets shorter while the building behind it gets bigger.

The energy also starts to pause on its own. Battery swapping replaces a vehicle’s battery in minutes instead of charging it in place. By February 2026 NIO had built 3,790 swap stations and completed 100 million swaps.<sup>40</sup> The driver leaves almost at once, but the battery left behind stays on site for hours while it recharges. The stop moves from the person to the energy.

This is where the Powerhouse earns its name. A charging site can hold energy as well as pass it on. With batteries on site, a fast-charging station can draw a steady, smaller supply from the grid and release it at speed when vehicles arrive. Appropriately sized battery-buffered systems can cut the grid capacity a station needs by about 50 to 80 per cent, and can keep chargers running through a power cut; the federal guidance gives the example of a station operating for up to ten hours without the grid.<sup>41</sup> Add generation on the site’s roofs and canopies, and the building becomes a small power plant for its neighbourhood: storing energy, smoothing demand and keeping the lights on when the network fails.

The architecture follows from three layers that change at different speeds. The energy layer (connection, storage and generation) needs to be reachable and replaceable, because batteries and power electronics wear out and improve far faster than buildings. The charging layer (bays, cables and chargers) will change with each generation of vehicle and standard. The public layer (rooms, courts and routes) should last for decades. Federal fleet guidance already asks operators to plan charging from vehicle schedules, battery sizes and dwell times rather than from the charger alone;<sup>42</sup> the Powerhouse applies the same logic to the building, keeping the long-lived public rooms independent of the short-lived equipment.

Faster charging does not empty the building. Some pauses are set by people, not batteries: a truck driver still needs thirty minutes off after eight hours of driving, and ten hours off at the end of the day.<sup>43</sup> A visit to a clinic, a reading room or a community event lasts as long as it lasts. The three stays from Chapter 1 still hold: twenty minutes, an hour or two, and a night. What changes is the overlap. The programme brings people in; the charge lets them stay, and as the charge shortens, the programme carries more of the reason to be there. People who arrive without a vehicle use the building in the same way.

These are the conditions of the pause. The ground already exists wherever vehicles stand. Charging is moving from homes to public sites, and growing. Every age has built a place for its pause, and today’s pause is set by vehicles, rules and the speed of the charger. As that speed rises, the site’s role as a store and source of power grows. Chapter 3 turns from the conditions to the place itself: what people need, what makes them stay, and how a public room can be recognised as one.

body: A railway station is never only a platform. Grand Central Terminal in New York is open to the public from early morning until two at night, and it holds restaurants, a food hall, a market and shops around the concourse where trains are never seen.<sup>1</sup> The airport has gone further. When Jewel opened at Singapore’s Changi Airport in 2019, its planners expected forty to fifty million visitors in the first year, most of them residents rather than travellers, coming for a forest valley and a waterfall seven storeys tall.<sup>2</sup> <sup>3</sup> John Kasarda describes the airport that grows a city of programmes around itself as the aerotropolis.<sup>4</sup> In both cases the transport function brings people to a building, and a network of other programmes turns that building into a destination.

Planning research has a name for this double role. In Luca Bertolini’s node–place model, a station area is at once a node, a point in the transport network, and a place, a part of the city with its own activities.5 Where the two are in proportion the area is balanced. Where transport outweighs everything else, the model calls it an unbalanced node: a location “where the transport systems are relatively more developed than the urban activities.”6 Almost every charging site built today is an unbalanced node. It is a strong point in the energy and road network, often fast and well connected, and almost nothing as a place.

The Powerhouse is proposed as the architecture that balances it. The charge makes it a node; the programme makes it a place. Section 2.3 traced how places of waiting worked in plan; this chapter asks what they hold. A station and an airport hold a mix: rooms for a few minutes, rooms for an hour, rooms for a night, some open to everyone and some run by an operator. A charging site has the movement and the time, but so far none of the mix. What the Powerhouse holds depends on the place: on what the people who live, work and travel nearby lack, on what keeps them comfortable while they stay, and on what would make the building worth visiting without a vehicle to charge.

body: Infrastructure is usually counted in pipes, cables and roads, but it also includes the places where people meet. Eric Klinenberg calls these places social infrastructure: libraries, parks, playgrounds, community rooms and even barbershops, the settings that decide whether strangers cross paths and come to rely on each other.<sup>7</sup> His study of the 1995 Chicago heat wave found that neighbourhoods with similar demographics and the same heat suffered very different death tolls, and that those with active streets, shops, organisations and gathering places lost fewer people, because neighbours knew to check on one another.<sup>8</sup>

The need is larger than a heat wave. In 2023 the US Surgeon General declared an epidemic of loneliness and isolation, reporting that about half of American adults experience loneliness.<sup>9</sup> Ray Oldenburg argued that third places, the café and the corner shop between home and work, were disappearing from American life, and with them the casual contact that holds a neighbourhood together.<sup>10</sup>

What people need from a public place can be named. Stephen Carr and his co-authors identify five needs that people bring to public space: comfort, relaxation, passive engagement with the scene around them, active engagement with other people, and discovery.11 William Whyte’s films showed the same needs at work: people sit where there is somewhere to sit, stay where there is food, shade and something to watch, and walk past everywhere else.12 For a Powerhouse the five needs translate into provision. Comfort means toilets, drinking water, shade and shelter. Relaxation means seating away from the bays. Passive engagement means a view of the life of the place. Active engagement means rooms to meet, eat, play and work. Discovery means a programme that changes: a market day, an exhibition, an event. Jan Gehl and Birgitte Svarre’s methods of counting who stays, where and for how long give the study a way to check whether the provisions work.13

body: Chapter 2 measured the pause by the charge. This section takes the opposite case: a Powerhouse that works even when no one is charging. If the building depended entirely on the length of a charge, faster chargers would empty it. A programme people use every day for its own sake keeps it full whatever the vehicles do.

Research on station areas shows how much this matters. A study of high-speed rail stations in China’s Yangtze River Delta found that station areas are shifting from a “transit place” to an “ultimate destination”, yet their planning neglects the non-travelling pedestrians who come for commerce, services, recreation and walking, and that it is these visitors who bring business and public life to a station area.<sup>14</sup> The same is true of a charging site. The people who come without a vehicle to charge are the ones who make it a place.

Japan’s roadside stations show the model at national scale. Since 1993 its Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism has designated michi-no-eki that combine free parking, toilets and rest for travellers with information and a facility for the local area: a market for local produce, a restaurant, a craft workshop or a community hall, run with the host municipality.15 There are now about 1,230 of them, and 79 have been designated as disaster-prevention stations with backup power, water and open ground for relief.16 Residents use them as everyday places, not only travellers.

The same test sorts the Powerhouse’s programme. Some uses stay busy all day without a single charging session: toilets, a covered plaza, a playground, a market or grocery, a parcel room, a laundromat, a clinic, a pharmacy, childcare and a cooling or emergency shelter. Others depend more on the people the charge brings: a waiting lounge, a café, rooms for drivers. A Powerhouse needs enough of the first kind that it would still be a place if every vehicle left.

body: People adopt new infrastructure more readily when it belongs to a place they care about. A review of research on renewable energy across Europe found that local acceptance turns less on the technology than on landscape character, attachment to place and trust in the process, and that a plant seen as a technical object dropped into a landscape is resisted most.<sup>17</sup> Charging is the visible part of the energy transition for most people, and today it looks like a row of posts in a car park.

Architecture can change that, and the iconic building is the strongest tool it has. Charles Jencks traced the rise of the iconic building, a form so distinctive that a building becomes a city’s emblem, and argued that its power lies in enigma: a striking form whose meaning stays open.<sup>18</sup> Frank Gehry’s Guggenheim Museum turned Bilbao into a destination and still drew 1,305,003 visitors in 2025, almost thirty years after it opened.<sup>19</sup> Bjarke Ingels Group’s CopenHill in Copenhagen applies the same ambition to energy itself: a 41,000-square-metre waste-to-energy plant whose roof is a public ski slope and hiking trail, with an 85-metre climbing wall on its façade.<sup>20</sup> <sup>21</sup> People come to ski or climb and leave knowing how their city’s energy is made.

The icon also has a critic. Leslie Sklair argues that today’s iconic buildings mostly serve private interests and consumption, whereas monumental architecture in the past “often had a strong public component.”<sup>22</sup> The Powerhouse takes that critique as its brief. It is meant to be an icon of the transition, a building people recognise, visit and are proud of, but an icon with the public component restored: its structure, roof and light make the energy visible, and its open ground and public rooms make it a place anyone can use. An icon without a public programme is a brand; with one, it is a civic building.

body: Most charging today happens on dark, hard ground. Conventional pavement absorbs the sun: in an Arizona pilot study cited by the EPA, asphalt reached 152°F (67°C) at mid-day, while cool pavements stayed 10 to 16°F cooler.<sup>23</sup> Paved surfaces and buildings hold that heat and release it into the evening, which is what makes cities hotter than their surroundings.<sup>24</sup> A driver waiting beside a charger on a summer afternoon is waiting on one of the hottest surfaces in the city.

The parking lot does not have to be like this. Eran Ben-Joseph’s study of its design and culture shows that parking lots can be aesthetically pleasing, environmentally and architecturally responsible, and used for something other than car storage.25 Green ground changes the experience most. The World Health Organization’s review of urban green space links it with better mental and physical health, lower stress, more physical activity and more social contact, as well as relief from heat, noise and air pollution.26 The EPA’s Green Streets Handbook, introduced in 2.1, treats parking surfaces as places to plant, shade and let rain soak in.27

The Powerhouse turns the ground it stands on into a community park. Trees and canopies shade the bays and the routes between them; planted ground takes the rain; lawns, gardens and a playground sit where people wait. CopenHill’s roof shows that an energy building can carry a park; the Powerhouse brings the park down to the ground people arrive on. The architecture makes the building’s sustainability visible: shade, water and planting are things people feel. A place that is cool, green and comfortable is one people choose to stay in.

body: A public building does not have to be open in every part at every hour. Keller Easterling argues that the rules built into infrastructure, its gates, payment systems and access controls, decide who may enter long before any law is invoked.<sup>28</sup> A charging station that can only be entered by car and unlocked with an app has already decided who it is for.

The Powerhouse sets its rules in layers. Its ground, routes, plaza, shade, seating, toilets and water are open to everyone, with nothing to buy and no vehicle needed. Some rooms keep set hours: a reading room, a community hall, a market. Others are run by an operator for the people they serve: a clinic, a gym, childcare, rooms for drivers on their required rest. These rooms are permanent parts of the building with their own entrances and hours, and closing them does not close the public ground around them.

This gradient lets the Powerhouse be both open and safe to run. The public layer is what makes it a civic building; the operated rooms are what make it useful every day; the charger serves both. The design question is where each layer sits: the open ground at the front and centre, the scheduled rooms around it, and the operated rooms where they can close without closing the place.
notes: Keller Easterling, Extrastatecraft: The Power of Infrastructure Space (London: Verso, 2014).

body: The sections above lead to a catalogue rather than a single brief. Table 3.1 sets out programmes a Powerhouse can hold, sorted three ways: by the length of stay they suit (the three stays from Chapter 1), by the setting where they are most likely to be needed (a freight corridor, a city, a town), and by access (open to all, set hours, or run by an operator). No site needs all of them. A corridor site might hold toilets, a food hall, showers and rooms for drivers; a city site a reading room, a gym and a workspace; a town site a clinic, a market and a hall.

The catalogue is the tool that balances the node. Each programme added from the table raises the place value of a site that the charger has already made a strong node, until the two are in proportion. Chapter 4 turns the catalogue into a framework: it asks what a particular place lacks, chooses from the table, and arranges the choices around the charger, using the three moves from section 2.3 and the access layers above. The Powerhouse is not a fixed building repeated along the road. It is a type that takes its programme from the place.

Public space stays alive when people have a recurring reason to use it. Chapter 3 showed that a charging stop can become social infrastructure if it is open without purchase and stitched into the fabric of its neighbourhood. Chapter 4 asks how the building is programmed, how it is paid for, and how it works across the twenty-four hours of the day. Working through social theory and sustainability, it brings together four ideas: the multimodal mobility hub with a civic room at its heart, the right of non-drivers and residents to shape the programme, the energy commons that lets local power and charging revenue sustain community uses, and the temporal rhythm that keeps the building active across every shift.

When a charging site is planned for cars alone, it isolates drivers from every other way people move. Planned instead as a neighbourhood mobility hub, it brings train, bus, bicycle, micromobility, walking, ride-hail and EV charging together around a shared civic room. In London, Foster + Partners’ Crossrail Place at Canary Wharf (2015) topped a new Elizabeth line railway station with four storeys of community rooms, shops and a public roof garden under a 310-metre timber lattice, uniting station, park and public hall in one section.1 Across Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium, municipal networks such as Bremen’s mobil.punkt hubs place car-sharing, cargo bikes, cycle parking, transit stops and neighbourhood services at a single street corner, while Carlos Moreno’s model of the “15-minute city” argues that daily essentials—work, food, healthcare, learning and leisure—should sit within a short walk or bike ride of every home.2

body: Henri Lefebvre’s “right to the city” is not merely the right to visit existing urban spaces, but the right of inhabitants to appropriate and shape the places of daily life outside the logic of commodity exchange.<sup>3</sup> Applied to transport infrastructure, it means a neighbourhood charging hub cannot be programmed solely around what extracts the highest spend per minute from a captive driver.

Instead, the programme is chosen by auditing what the surrounding radius lacks. Where a neighbourhood is underserved by healthcare, fresh food, study space or youth facilities, the Powerhouse allocates floor area to a community clinic, a fresh-produce market, a library reading room or after-school studios alongside commercial anchor tenants.
notes: Henri Lefebvre, “The Right to the City,” in Writings on Cities, ed. and trans. Eleonore Kofman and Elizabeth Lebas (Oxford: Blackwell, 1996), 147–159.

body: Because different vehicles and errands bring different people, the Powerhouse serves overlapping publics that rarely share a building today: morning rail and bus commuters, long-haul and local delivery drivers taking mandated rest breaks, ride-hail and taxi drivers between shifts, apartment residents charging a car or e-bike, schoolchildren in the afternoon, and older residents visiting a clinic or park.

Designing for all of them in one section turns Jane Jacobs’s principle of “eyes on the street” into an interior and rooftop condition: a charging deck or rest stop that would feel isolated and unsafe at night becomes active and self-policing when it shares its hall with a 24-hour community and mobility hub.<sup>4</sup>
notes: Jane Jacobs, The Death and Life of Great American Cities (New York: Random House, 1961), 35–54.

body: How does a charging hub fund public space and community rooms without turning into a shopping mall? The answer lies in treating local energy generation and charging as an energy commons: infrastructure owned in whole or in part by the public and the community it serves.

Three models show how this works in practice. First, municipal ownership: CopenHill in Copenhagen was built for an energy company owned by five local municipalities, allowing capital investment in clean energy to deliver a major public park on its roof.5 Second, community equity shares: in the South Bronx, the MN8 Gateway to Hunts Point freight-charging hub (scheduled for ~2029) pairs high-power commercial truck and car charging with a community solar array serving roughly 300 local households, structured so that 50 percent of the project is community-owned.6 Third, neighbourhood microgrids: projects such as the Brooklyn Microgrid allow rooftop solar producers and battery hosts to trade local electricity directly with neighbours and feed resilience power back into the local grid during peak demand.7 At the Powerhouse, rooftop solar, stationary battery storage and commercial fast-charging fees cross-subsidise free civic space and affordable community rooms.

body: Cities run on rhythms: morning commutes, school bells, delivery shifts, evening gatherings and overnight rest. In What Time Is This Place? (1972), Kevin Lynch urged architects and planners to treat time as a design material as real as space, and in Rhythmanalysis (2004), Henri Lefebvre showed how urban life is produced by the intersection of cyclical daily rhythms and linear work schedules.8

Most monofunctional buildings sit empty for half the twenty-four-hour cycle: office car parks empty at 6 pm, residential garages empty at 9 am, and highway forecourts go quiet overnight. By matching its programme to the four lengths of stop established in Chapter 2 and the four six-hour windows of the urban day, the Powerhouse stays active around the clock (Table 4.2).
notes: Kevin Lynch, What Time Is This Place? (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 1972); Henri Lefebvre, Rhythmanalysis: Space, Time and Everyday Life, trans. Stuart Elden and Gerald Moore (London: Continuum, 2004).

body: A building designed for a twenty-to-sixty-minute stop must also be ready for a future in which batteries charge in five minutes or autonomous vehicles drop passengers at the door and park themselves elsewhere. As Stan Allen argued in “Infrastructural Urbanism,” architecture endures when it provides a robust spatial field whose servicing and structural grid can host changing programmes without demolition.<sup>9</sup>

Because the Powerhouse is conceived as a monumental civic station with soaring structural spans, vaulted ceiling heights, and integrated utility spines, its civic armature endures across evolutionary cycles: spaces dedicated to rapid fleet charging today can seamlessly rebalance into expanded public atriums, community fabrication labs, or grid-scale battery chambers as autonomous operations and solid-state charging accelerate.
Summary

The Powerhouse elevates the technical necessity of electric vehicle fast charging into an inspiring architectural marvel and civic station for New York. Anchored by a multimodal transit cathedral, governed by open public rules, sustained by a community energy commons, and programmed across all twenty-four hours of the day, it transforms a technical pause in transport into lasting monumental infrastructure.
